The Forward Deployed Engineer internship in short

In the SkillMe Forward Deployed Engineer internship you build ClientBridge: Third-Party API Integration Dashboard, a project where you wrap a real third-party API into a small internal tool for a 'client', complete with a config-driven dashboard, runbook docs, and handling for the messy edge cases real integrations hit. In week 1 you pick a real public API (weather, currency exchange, GitHub, or similar) and build a clean Python wrapper around it, as if you were the engineer a client hired to 'just make this API work for us'. By week 4 you package the whole integration the way you'd actually hand it to a client team: clear setup docs, a runbook for common issues, and a short demo. Each milestone is posted on LinkedIn and checked against that week's checklist before it counts. Top performers earn a stipend of up to $100 a month.

Week by week

What each week of the Forward Deployed Engineer internship covers

The four milestones of ClientBridge: Third-Party API Integration Dashboard.

  1. Week 1 of 4

    Wrapping a Third-Party API

    Beginner2-3 hours

    Pick a real public API (weather, currency exchange, GitHub, or similar) and build a clean Python wrapper around it, as if you were the engineer a client hired to 'just make this API work for us'. This is the core skill of forward-deployed work: making someone else's API usable and reliable.

    What you learn

    • Reading third-party API docs and identifying auth requirements and rate limits
    • Wrapping raw HTTP calls in a small client class with clear methods
    • Handling API errors, timeouts and rate limits gracefully
    • Keeping API keys out of code with .env and python-dotenv

    What you submit

    • An ApiClient class wrapping at least 2 real endpoints of a chosen third-party API
    • Custom error handling with a clear ApiClientError for failures
    • Basic retry logic for transient errors
    • A CLI script proving the client works against the live API
    How week 1 is reviewed
    • Calling each client method with valid input returns clean, correctly-typed Python data
    • A deliberately invalid input (bad city, bad symbol) raises ApiClientError with a readable message, not a raw traceback
    • The API key never appears anywhere in committed code or Git history
    • The CLI script runs successfully end to end against the live API

    Stretch goal: Add response caching (an in-memory dict keyed by request params, with a 5-minute expiry) to avoid hitting rate limits during repeated testing.

  2. Week 2 of 4

    Config-Driven Dashboard for a 'Client'

    Beginner+2-3 hours

    Turn last week's API wrapper into a small internal dashboard for an imagined client, where what's shown is driven by a config file rather than hardcoded — because real clients always want to add or change tracked items without you editing code every time.

    What you learn

    • Designing a simple config file format (JSON or YAML) to drive an app's behaviour
    • Building a lightweight dashboard UI with Streamlit
    • Separating configuration from code so non-engineers could plausibly edit it
    • Displaying live data pulled through your Week 1 API client

    What you submit

    • A config.json/config.yaml describing tracked items for a fictional client
    • A load_config function with clear validation errors
    • A Streamlit dashboard showing live data per config entry with a manual refresh
    • Graceful per-row error handling for one bad config entry
    How week 2 is reviewed
    • Editing config.json to add or remove a tracked item changes the dashboard without any code changes
    • The dashboard clearly shows when data was last refreshed
    • A config with one invalid entry (bad city/symbol) still renders the dashboard for the valid entries, with a visible error for the bad one
    • Running load_config on a config missing a required key raises a clear, specific error

    Stretch goal: Add a config field for a per-item alert threshold (e.g. temperature above X, exchange rate above Y) and highlight rows that cross it.

  3. Week 3 of 4

    Edge Cases, Support Scenarios and Logging

    Intermediate2-3 hours

    Simulate the messy reality of supporting a live integration: rate limits, partial outages, malformed client configs, and a support ticket asking 'why is this wrong?'. This week is about building the resilience and observability that separates a demo from something a client can actually depend on.

    What you learn

    • Simulating and handling rate-limit and outage scenarios
    • Structured logging for debugging a live integration after the fact
    • Writing a support-style root-cause investigation from logs alone
    • Defensive config validation against realistic client mistakes

    What you submit

    • Structured request/error logging across the API client and dashboard
    • Simulated rate-limit handling with backoff-and-retry
    • Graceful degradation during a simulated partial outage
    • 3 written root-cause investigations based only on log evidence
    • A diagnostics view reporting API health and recent errors
    How week 3 is reviewed
    • Running with rate-limit simulation on shows retries in the log and the app still completes successfully
    • A simulated outage on one item shows a clear 'stale data' warning in the dashboard rather than a crash
    • All 3 support-ticket root-cause notes correctly identify the actual injected cause using only the logs
    • The diagnostics view accurately reflects a deliberately broken item's status

    Stretch goal: Add a simple alerting rule: if an item has been failing for more than N minutes, write a highlighted line to a separate alerts.log.

  4. Week 4 of 4

    Setup Docs, Runbook and Client Handoff

    Intermediate+2-3 hours

    Package the whole integration the way you'd actually hand it to a client team: clear setup docs, a runbook for common issues, and a short demo. This week is entirely about the documentation and polish that make forward-deployed work usable by people who didn't build it.

    What you learn

    • Writing setup documentation for a non-engineer or junior engineer audience
    • Writing an operational runbook: common issues, symptoms, and fixes
    • Structuring a handoff so someone else could operate the tool without you
    • Presenting a technical integration clearly to a non-technical stakeholder

    What you submit

    • A SETUP.md verified by an outside walkthrough with fixes applied
    • A RUNBOOK.md covering at least 5 realistic operational issues
    • A known-limitations section and a one-page non-technical client summary
    • A 2-3 minute demo video showing the dashboard and a live runbook scenario
    How week 4 is reviewed
    • Someone unfamiliar with the project can get the dashboard running using only SETUP.md
    • RUNBOOK.md has at least 5 issues each with symptom, cause and fix
    • The client summary is understandable without any code or API knowledge
    • The demo video shows one real failure scenario being diagnosed using the runbook

    Stretch goal: Turn RUNBOOK.md into an interactive checklist inside the dashboard itself (a 'Troubleshooting' tab listing the same issues and fixes).

Forward Deployed Engineer internship: questions and answers

What will I build in the Forward Deployed Engineer internship?

You build ClientBridge: Third-Party API Integration Dashboard. Wrap a real third-party API into a small internal tool for a 'client', complete with a config-driven dashboard, runbook docs, and handling for the messy edge cases real integrations hit. It is one project built up over four weekly milestones, so each week adds to the last.

What skills will I learn in the Forward Deployed Engineer internship?

The Forward Deployed Engineer internship works with API Integration, Client Tools and Docs. Week 1: reading third-party API docs and identifying auth requirements and rate limits; wrapping raw HTTP calls in a small client class with clear methods. Week 2: designing a simple config file format (JSON or YAML) to drive an app's behaviour; building a lightweight dashboard UI with Streamlit. Week 3: simulating and handling rate-limit and outage scenarios; structured logging for debugging a live integration after the fact. Week 4: writing setup documentation for a non-engineer or junior engineer audience; writing an operational runbook: common issues, symptoms, and fixes.

Do I need experience to apply for the Forward Deployed Engineer internship?

You need the basics of API Integration, Client Tools and Docs, not prior internship experience. Week 1 starts at beginner level, where you pick a real public API (weather, currency exchange, GitHub, or similar) and build a clean Python wrapper around it, as if you were the engineer a client hired to 'just make this API work for us'. Week 4 reaches intermediate+ level. A short screening quiz (8 questions, about 5 minutes) checks you are ready to start.

How is each Forward Deployed Engineer milestone reviewed?

Every week has a checklist, and a milestone is approved only when it meets all of it. For week 1 of ClientBridge: Third-Party API Integration Dashboard, that means: calling each client method with valid input returns clean, correctly-typed Python data; a deliberately invalid input (bad city, bad symbol) raises ApiClientError with a readable message, not a raw traceback; the API key never appears anywhere in committed code or Git history; the CLI script runs successfully end to end against the live API. Reviewers include engineers who work at Walmart, Google and LinkedIn, and work that misses the bar comes back with notes.

What can I put on my resume after the Forward Deployed Engineer internship?

Each approved milestone gives you a line you can back up with a public LinkedIn post: Built a clean Python wrapper around a real third-party API with proper error handling; Added retry logic for transient network failures in an API client; Learned to turn a raw external API into a reliable internal tool; Built a config-driven internal dashboard so a client could add tracked items without code changes; Designed a validated config file format for a small internal tool; Handled partial failures gracefully so one bad config entry didn't break the whole dashboard; Simulated rate limits and partial outages to test an integration's resilience; Added structured logging and a diagnostics view for debugging a live client tool; Practiced support-style root-cause investigation using only application logs; Wrote setup docs and a runbook that let someone else operate my integration without me; Validated my own onboarding docs with a real outside walkthrough and fixed the gaps found; Presented a technical client integration clearly to a non-technical audience.

Is the Forward Deployed Engineer internship paid? Is there a stipend?

Top performers earn a stipend of up to $100 a month. It is performance-based and goes to the interns whose reviewed Forward Deployed Engineer work stands out in their cohort, not to every intern.

How much time does it take?

4 weeks, one milestone a week, each planned for about 2-3 hours. It is fully remote and open worldwide, so you work around college or a job.
